Feluda.description: A private investigator and the protagonist of the stories, known for his sharp intellect and often addressed respectfully as Felu Babu.

Lalmohan Babu.description: A popular thriller writer and companion of Feluda, also known by his pen name Jatayu.

Tulsi Babu.description: A retired schoolteacher living in Gosaipur and an old acquaintance of Lalmohan Babu.

Jeevanlal Mallik.description: The son of Shyamlal Mallik who invites Feluda to Gosaipur to investigate matters at the Mallik household.

Shyamlal Mallik.description: Jeevanlal's father and a former zamindar who has rejected modern life after an accident.

Ganga.description: Ganga is Tulsi Babu's servant who helps with household chores.

Suresh Chakladar.description: A barrister who presides over local functions in Gosaipur.

Mriganka Bhattacharya.description: A local figure reputed to communicate with spirits, also known as Atmaram or Atmaram Babu, who is eventually arrested for theft.

Gosaipur.description: A fictional village in Bengal where much of the story is set.

Victoria Memorial.description: A famous monument and museum in Kolkata, built in memory of Queen Victoria.

Princep Ghat.description: A historic riverside ghat along the Hooghly River in Kolkata.

Sandesh.description: A Bengali children's magazine, historically edited by Satyajit Ray and his family.

Gosaipur Literary Society.description: A local organization in Gosaipur that arranges literary events and receptions.

Katwa Junction.description: A real railway junction in West Bengal, serving as a transit point to Gosaipur.

Calcutta.description: The former name of Kolkata, the capital city of West Bengal.

National Geographic.description: A well-known international magazine focused on geography, history, and world culture.

Canada.description: A country in North America, referenced as Feluda's supposed place of residence.

Azimganj.description: A town in West Bengal, mentioned as the residence of Tulsi Babu's married daughter.

daalmut.description: A crunchy Indian snack made from fried lentils and spices.

rickshaw.description: A small, two- or three-wheeled passenger vehicle pulled by a person or driven by cycle.

kurta.description: A traditional long shirt worn in South Asia.

dhoti.description: A traditional Indian garment for men, consisting of a long piece of cloth wrapped around the waist and legs.

palanquin.description: A covered litter for one passenger, carried on poles by several bearers.

punkha-puller.description: A person employed to manually operate a ceiling fan (punkha) by pulling a cord, especially before electric fans.

cheroots.description: A type of cigar with both ends clipped during manufacture, popular in South Asia.

neem.description: A tree native to India, whose twigs are often used as natural toothbrushes.

ayurvedic.description: Relating to Ayurveda, the traditional system of medicine native to India.

Kaviraj.description: A traditional Ayurvedic doctor or herbal healer.

beaten-rice.description: Also known as 'poha', flattened rice flakes commonly eaten as a snack or breakfast in India.

veranda.description: A roofed, open-air porch or gallery attached to the outside of a house.

bamboo grove.description: A small forested area consisting mainly of bamboo plants.

zamindar.description: A landowner, especially one who leases land to tenant farmers; historically, a hereditary aristocrat in Bengal.

citation.description: A formal statement of praise or recognition, often presented at a public function.

seances.description: Meetings at which people attempt to communicate with spirits of the dead.

Topshe.description: Feluda's cousin and the narrator of the stories, who assists in investigations.

Dashu.description: A servant in the Mallik household, responsible for pulling the fan.

Bholanath Babu.description: The trusted manager of the Mallik household, originally from the village.

Durlabh Singh Mallik.description: Shyamlal Mallik's father, a ruthless and feared figure in Gosaipur's history.

Tarak Kaviraj.description: The ayurvedic doctor attending to Shyamlal Mallik.

Ramayana.description: An ancient Indian epic depicting the life and adventures of Lord Rama.

Bengali.description: A language spoken in the Indian state of West Bengal and Bangladesh; some books in the house are in Bengali.

Nescafé.description: A popular brand of instant coffee.

south India.description: A region in the southern part of India, referenced in relation to drinking coffee.

Katwa.description: A town mentioned as the posting location of the threatening letter.

bearer.description: A household servant, often responsible for serving and carrying items.

hookah.description: A traditional Indian water pipe used for smoking, common in South Asia. The plural form is hookahs.

bolster.description: A long, firm pillow placed under other pillows for support.

Nityanand.description: Mr Bhattacharya's nephew who assists him in spiritual matters.

Kali.description: A Hindu goddess often associated with destruction and power, worshipped in many parts of India.

Guatemala.description: A country in Central America, mentioned by Lalmohan Babu as a potential setting for his novel.

Mitter.description: Feluda's surname, used formally in the text.

moong daal.description: A dish made from split yellow mung beans, commonly eaten in Indian cuisine.

Odomos.description: A popular Indian brand of mosquito repellent cream.

Lakshmi.description: Bholanath Babu's deceased daughter, whose spirit was supposedly contacted by Mriganka Bhattacharya.

Jagarani.description: The local club in the village, involved in organizing and rehearsing plays.

Charminar.description: A popular Indian brand of cigarettes smoked by Feluda.

Dettol.description: A well-known antiseptic liquid used for cleaning wounds.

shaluk.description: An aquatic flower, commonly known as water lily, found in ponds in Bengal.

paan.description: A preparation combining betel leaf with areca nut and sometimes tobacco, chewed for its stimulant effects.

mosquito net.description: A fine mesh net used to protect against mosquito bites while sleeping.

Jeevanlal’s grandmother.description: An elderly woman living in the rear portion of the house, unaware of the murder.

Kali temple.description: A Hindu temple dedicated to the goddess Kali, mentioned as a landmark near the bamboo grove. The Bat-kali temple is an old, abandoned Kali temple in the village, now inhabited by bats and considered a local attraction.

Babu.description: A respectful suffix or form of address for men in Bengali and Hindi.

chappals.description: A type of open-toed sandal commonly worn in India.

saree.description: A traditional garment worn by women in India, consisting of a long piece of cloth draped around the body.

Sudhakar Pramanik.description: The police inspector in charge of the investigation who helps recover stolen money and is initially skeptical of Feluda.

Malliks.description: A family in Gosaipur who own a garden believed to be a breeding ground for mosquitoes.

Uri Geller.description: A real-life Israeli-British illusionist famous for allegedly bending spoons and forks with his mind.

Benimadhav.description: A mime artist encountered by the protagonists near the bamboo grove; he offers to show them the Bat-kali temple and reacts dramatically upon discovering a dead body.

beedi.description: A thin, hand-rolled cigarette made of tobacco wrapped in a tendu or temburni leaf, commonly smoked in India.

pyjamas.description: Loose-fitting trousers, often worn as nightwear or casual attire in South Asia.

dakaat.description: A term for 'dacoit,' meaning a bandit or armed robber in India.

tabla.description: A pair of Indian drums used in classical and popular music.

shloka.description: A verse, phrase, proverb, or hymn typically composed in Sanskrit, often used in religious or philosophical contexts.

mango tree.description: A culturally significant tree in India, often referenced in stories and used as a landmark.
